title: The runaway horse
hook: idle, his mind bolted like a runaway horse, so he wrote down its fancies to shame it (Essays 1.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, painted beams: sayings over Montaigne's head while he wrote. Your line was on the beams. Did you put a line where you'd see it, and did you read it? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

The plan was rest. A long weekend, nothing booked, phone on the counter. And by Saturday afternoon the mind has replayed an argument from last spring, drafted a resignation letter, priced a boat, and worried about a mole. Stillness was supposed to be quiet. Instead it's loud, like a radio left on in an empty house. Montaigne hit exactly this wall right after he climbed into his tower, and he wrote a short essay about it.
screen: `THE PLAN WAS REST.` → `THE MIND GETS LOUD.` → `MONTAIGNE HITS THE WALL.`

segments.voice: First, the field. The essay is called Of idleness, and it opens on farmland. A rich field left fallow, he says, doesn't stay empty. It fills with wild weeds. To be useful, it has to be sown. A mind is the same. Leave it with nothing to hold, and it grows its own crop. Second, the horse. When he retired, Montaigne says, he thought the kindest thing he could do for his mind was to leave it alone, to let it rest and settle into itself. It did the opposite. Like a runaway horse, he says, it gave itself a hundred times more free rein than it ever took for anyone else. It bred strange creatures and monsters, one after another, with no order and no point. Third, the trick. He didn't fight the horse. He started writing down what it threw up, so he could look at those odd fancies at leisure. And his stated hope was a little sly: that in time, seeing them on paper, his mind would be ashamed of itself. Fourth, why this matters. Here is a man in a tower with every comfort for thinking, admitting his thinking ran wild. Some readers find the seed of the whole book in that honesty: in this essay, at least, he says his writing began as notes on a mind that wouldn't sit still. Off the page, the runaway horse is the three a.m. spiral, or the shower where you win an argument nobody's having. Montaigne's move is plain: don't chase it, write it down, and look at it in daylight.
screen: `A FALLOW FIELD GROWS WEEDS.` · `THE MIND BOLTS LIKE A HORSE.` · `WRITE ITS FANCIES DOWN.` · `THE BOOK BEGINS THERE.` · then, large: `THE RUNAWAY HORSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down your wandering thoughts. Have something to write on nearby. Sit, and let the breath slow. Then let the horse run. Don't steer it. Each time you notice a thought has carried you off, a worry, a plan, a memory, a song, jot two or three words for it and come back to the breath. A grocery item. A name. A what-if. No judging, no fixing. Just a list of where the horse went. The bell holds the time.
The runaway horse. Montaigne's picture of his idle mind: left to rest, it bolted and bred fancy after fancy, so he wrote them down to look at in daylight. Today's word.
Your line: the runaway horse. Today, when your mind bolts, don't chase it. Write three words about where it went, and read them later. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne point to his essay Of idleness as an account of how the Essays began: a restless mind, written down so it could be looked at calmly.

myth: Montaigne says resting in his tower calmed his mind at once
it did the opposite: his mind bolted like a runaway horse.
he says a fallow field fills with wild weeds
a rich field left unsown grows its own crop; so does an idle mind.
Montaigne tried to force his wandering thoughts out
he wrote them down, to look at them at leisure and, he hoped, shame his mind.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne, newly retired. you left your mind free to rest, and it's running wild with fancies. what do you do?
options: fill every hour with company to drown it out.
start writing the fancies down to look at them.
give up the tower and go back to court.
fork.reveal: he began putting his mind's odd fancies on paper, to study them at leisure and in time make his mind ashamed of itself.

original.note: French: a runaway horse, Montaigne's picture of his idle mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the runaway horse is about losing your temper.
what it means: an idle mind doesn't go quiet; it bolts, and writing its fancies down is how Montaigne looked at them.
what a scholar hears: by Montaigne's own account in this short essay, his writing began as a way of watching his own restless mind.

sources.ref: Essays 1.8, Of idleness (fallow fields grow weeds; his idle mind, like a runaway horse, bred chimeras and monsters; he began to write them down to shame it)

notes: Essays 1.8 paraphrased throughout. 'A hundred times more trouble' is Montaigne's own figure in the essay; confirm it survives in the paraphrase as his wording.
Original 'cheval échappé' follows Montaigne's phrase 'faisant le cheval eschappé' in modern spelling; confirm.

'The essays began, by his own account, as notes on a mind that wouldn't sit still' rests on this essay's closing; some scholars read it as a literary pose rather than literal history. A Keeper may want to soften.

Editor: corrected the runaway-horse line (Montaigne's 'cent fois plus de carrière' is free rein, not trouble) and cut the misplaced 'a hundred fancies' from the word; softened 'the seed of the whole book' to some readers' view, tied to this essay; softened 'readers often'; varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn.
